messages.subject: Re: Error from suggest.buffer
messages.body_plain:
Examining your capthistW (received offline - thanks) I see that for each session (years 2019, 2021?) the traps object is the same and includes twice as many detectors as actually used in either year. As most locations matched in the two years, each detector appears to have a very close neighbor. This leads to the 2-m mean distance-to-nearest-other-detector, which in turn trips up the ad hoc algorithm in suggest.buffer() (and causes it to take an awfully long time). The solution is to provide the detector locations as two separate input files, one per session. Then the number of detectors per session will halve to 66.

I hope this helps.
Murray

messages.body_plain:
Hi Murray,

We are planning some fieldwork next year looking at snowshoe hare densities in different habitat configurations and started doing some exploring of different trapping designs to help design our study.

We are started with some "simple" configurations of density because we are interested in how density varies with different habitat configurations. The code below will generate a uniform density, a density gradient that declines linearly (B0 + B1*distance) from a horizontal linear feature, and a density gradient that declines in a negative exponential manner (B0*exp(-B1*distance) from a linear feature.

We can make our trapping grid, masks (with density gradients) and simulation scenarios, but we are simply stuck how to move forward with the actual simulations. We are interested in 3 things:

1. how do we specify the linear (I think that's just a function of the covariate for distance from the linear feature) and negative exponential models (some higher order polynomial to get close to the negative exponential shape?) for the density gradient?

2. how can we compare three models using AIC to see which one is chosen as the best model. That is, for each density gradient, which model (uniform, linear gradient, exponential gradient) is chosen.

2. how do we extract beta coefficients from the simulations (B0 and B1)?

Maybe our goals are too lofty for secrdesign? Should we just use other functions like sim.popn and secr.fit in a loop and save output in a list?

We have spent a good bit of time reading through your secrdesign manual and the vignettes but are stuck at this point. Any help in pointing us in the right direction would be appreciated!

Below is code that creates the density gradients and scenarios.

Duane

>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>>

library(secrdesign)
library(secr)
library(rgeos)
library(raster)
library(dplyr)
########### Inputs for simulation scenarios
 nx <- 40
 ny <- 40
 spacing <- 50
 side <- 2000
 x <- rep(0, 2000/spacing)
 y <- rep(2000, 2000/spacing)
 nrepl <- 4
 noccasions <- c(1)

########## Create trap and mask objects for simulation scenarios
 # trap.tran  <- make.transect(x=x, y=y)
 trap.grid  <- make.grid(nx=nx, ny=ny, spacing = spacing, detector="multi", originxy= c(0,0))
 trapset <- list(grid = trap.grid)

### Making a mask around the trap grid with a buffer of sigma
sigma <- 100
maskset <- make.mask(trap.grid, buffer = sigma)

### Calculating distance from each point in mask to a feature
rast <- raster(maskset) # turn mask into raster layer
# creating a horizontal line feature halfway thru plot
xcoord <- c(min(maskset$y),max(maskset$x)) # need to reference max and min to compensate for buffer
ycoord <- max(maskset$y)/2
feat <- sp::Line(cbind(xcoord,ycoord))
feat <- sp::Lines(list(feat),ID='A')
feat <- sp::SpatialLines(list(feat))
points <- as(rast,"SpatialPoints") # convert raster to points
dist <- gDistance(points,feat,byid=TRUE) # calc distance from each point to feature
values(rast) <- dist # assign these dist values to the raster layer
plot(rast) # plot
plot(feat,add=T)

# D1 is constant
D1 <- rep(4,nrow(maskset))
plot(D1)

# D2 is linear
a2 <- 4
b2 <- -4/max(dist) # make D go to 0 at max distance away from feature
D2 <- as.vector(a2+b2*abs(dist))
plot(D2)

# D2 is neg exp with steeper curve
a3 <- 4
b3 <- -0.005
D3 <- as.vector(a3*exp(b3*abs(dist)))
plot(D3)

# Assign these as covariates to the mask
covariates(maskset) <- data.frame(
  D1 = D1,
  D2 = D2,
  D3 = D3
)

# Visualizing mask and trap grid
  plot(maskset)
  plot(trap.grid, add = T)

# Make a list of pop models
pop <- list(list(model2D = "IHP", D = "D1"),
            list(model2D = "IHP", D = "D2"),
            list(model2D = "IHP", D = "D3"))

########## Specify and run simulations
 Scen1 <- make.scenarios(
  trapsindex = 1,
  noccasions = noccasions,
  g0 = 0.2,
  sigma = 100,
  crosstraps = TRUE,
  popindex = 1:3
)

scenarioSummary(Scen1, trapset)
# for 2 trap sets, 2 occasion numbers, and 3 density models, there are 12 scenarios

Scen1$maskindex <- c(1)

Run.Scen2 <- run.scenarios(
  1,
  scenarios = Scen1,
  trapset = trapset,
  maskset = maskset,
  pop.args = pop,
  fit.args = list(detectfn = "HHN"),
  det.arg = list(savepopn = TRUE),
  extractfn = identity
)
summary(Run.Scen2)

## find the simulated populations
pop1 <- attr(Run.Scen2$output[[1]][[1]], "popn")
pop2 <- attr(Run.Scen2$output[[2]][[1]], "popn")
pop3 <- attr(Run.Scen2$output[[3]][[1]], "popn")

## plot all to show run scenerio did what we want
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
plot(
  maskset,
  covariate = "D1")
plot(
  pop1,
  frame = FALSE,
  add = TRUE,
  col = "blue",
  pch = 16,
  cex = 0.6
)

plot(
  maskset,
  covariate = "D2"
)
plot(
  pop2,
  frame = FALSE,
  add = TRUE,
  col = "blue",
  pch = 16,
  cex = 0.6
)
plot(
  maskset,
  covariate = "D3"
)
plot(
  pop3,
  frame = FALSE,
  add = TRUE,
  col = "blue",
  pch = 16,
  cex = 0.6
)

## try to extract the trap grids and capture histor

messages.body_plain:
Duane

I'm glad you seem to have found a way through. You spurred me yesterday to add code to secrdesign for multi-model inference*, and that is almost ready to go. Yes, only linear models are supported in 'secr', with the partial exception of regression splines. Extracting coefficients is simple enough, using coef() as the extractfn, or applying it post hoc to whole model fits saved with extractfn identity() or trim().

Murray

* I had to strike a balance between functionality and adding more complexity to an already diverse package. The approach is to define multiple models for a single scenario fitindex, fit each of them to a given capthist at each replicate, and apply the extractfn to the bundle (secrlist) of fitted models. This usually requires either extractfn = modelAverage or a custom extractfn or downstream processing of the whole secrlist saved with extractfn = identity. A typical custom function would apply predict() to the AIC-best model.

I can offer sympathy, but not much insight. There seems to be a real problem with that model, so either the data were inadequate (for the complexity of the given model) or there was a numerical problem. Numerical problems can sometimes be solved by messing around with alternative algorithms (method = 'Nelder-Mead'?) or starting values.
Murray
P.S. Technically method = 'none' _only_ recomputes the variance-covariance matrix, so 're-fitting' is not accurate despite the re-use of secr.fit().

Hi all,

I wanted to jump in and note that I was running into a similar error using secr on my MacBook Pro M1. I am using secr version 4.5.8. Some models ran, but others produced this error. It tended to show up more often when I estimated more parameters in the model, but overall it is unpredictable.

For example, this model would run:
m9W <- secr.fit(capthistW, model = list(D~1, g0~1, sigma~session), buffer = 10000, CL = FALSE, detectfn = 0, method = "Newton-Raphson")
But this model would produce an error:
m6W <- secr.fit(capthistW, model = list(D~1, g0~1, sigma~h2), buffer = 10000, CL = FALSE, detectfn = 0, method = "Newton-Raphson")

Following Murray's earlier suggestion, specifying details = list(fastproximity = FALSE) solved the problem. So luckily there is a workaround, but it did significantly increase the run time. Happy to provide more information if helpful.

Best,
Elizabeth

messages.subject: Choosing between hcov models
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have some questions on how to make an informed decision about selecting finite mixture models vs. hybrid mixture models. We fit a series of SECR models on black bears with sex ID's. We fit one set of models with hcov = "sex" and another set with without hcov (some of which included regular heterogeneity and some of which included session, labelled as 'yr'). I have included screenshots of tables with the models, their AIC values, and density estimates.

As I understand it, the AIC values of models with hcov cannot be compared to other models. As can be seen in the table, though, the models which include latent classes produce significantly different estimates for density. I am not sure why the estimates would be so different, and I was wondering if there is guidance about whether hybrid or finite mixture models are better suited to certain kinds of studies.

Any help would be greatly appreciated. Thank you so much for your time.

All the best,
Elizabeth

messages.body_plain:
Hi
I can't say exactly why the estimates are so different, but it is not too surprising: the 'hcov' approach deals only with heterogeneity due to sex, whereas the finite mixture model (h2) adapts to unmodelled heterogeneity from any source (including e.g. age). I was a bit suspicious that the top h2 model had twice the density of the next model, but that is probably coincidental.

You can directly compare a finite mixture model and a sex-effect model when CL = FALSE. Thus, using built-in data

library(secr)
msk <- make.mask(traps(ovenCHp[[1]]), buffer=250, nx=20)
fithcov  <- secr.fit(ovenCHp[[1]], mask = msk, model=g0~h2, hcov='Sex', trace=F)
fitCLsex <- secr.fit(ovenCHp[[1]], mask = msk, model=g0~Sex, trace=F, CL = TRUE)
fitCLh2  <- secr.fit(ovenCHp[[1]], mask = msk, model=g0~h2, trace=F, CL = TRUE)

# direct comparison OK:
AIC(fitCLsex, fitCLh2)
